title: Canada, China agree to ease tariffs amid trade rows with US
summary: The Canadian and Chinese leaders have vowed closer cooperation as both nations seek to reduce reliance on the US. Canada's government said it had agreed to further reduce tariffs on a range of…

image.caption: Carney (L) and Xi held talks ahead of the APEC summit in ShenzhenImage: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen have produced deals to further reduce tariffs, Ottawa said on Tuesday.

The agreements reflect a growing rapprochement between the two countries after years of strained relations, thanks totrade tensions with Washington leading both Canada and China to seek to reduce dependence on the US.

At the talks, Carney hailed "greater predictability and stability" in ‌relations with China, while Xi said the cooperation between his country and Canada would "benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world."
Carney said Canada had already made faster-than-expected progress toward its goal of boosting exports to China "by 50% by the end of this decade."
What have China and Canada agreed on?
According to a statement from the Canadian government, China is to reduce tariffs on Canadian pork, fish and seafood.
In exchange, Canada will prolong the current tariff exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum for another two years.
The two leaders also agreed to cooperate more closely on economic and financial matters, and to work together in the fields of education and environmental protection.
Canada is too reliant on the United States, Carney tells DW
Xi and Carney already declared their intention to enhance bilateral ties during talks in Beijing in January.
There, they struck a deal that foresaw a reduction in tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, while Chinese electric vehicles gained easier access to the Canadian market.
Critics in Canada have, however, pointed out what they see as dangers to the country's security and values through the closer ties to Beijing.
Among other things, Canadian intelligence believes that China interfered in at least two federal elections, something Beijing denies.
